messages.author: 2af7908f1e86a1c4
messages.subject: Proposal idea: Interactive visualisations with SVG/HTML5 instead of Java
parts:
Hello,

I'm interested in taking part in the Summer of Code for R project. I have seen
an appealing task in the ideas list, namely interactive plottings, which is
something I always wanted R to have. However, on the initial outline there, I
got the idea that R mentors want to use Java applets for this. I'd like to
offer an alternative implementation in SVG/HTML5. The main pro's over the Java
approach are:
- Readily available in most browsers without plugins;
- Available on every platform a browser may run;
- May be rendered with hardware accelleration, including but not limited to
OpenVG API etc. This could turn out to be handy if we consider the handhelds
and tablets which are emerging worldwide as a handy and accessible tool.
- No relation to patented technology = no affilation with Oracle's patent
trolling (just in case);
Here's how I see it, we have a graphical device which outputs SVG code, much
like R-Cairo's vector output generator. However, extra data is embedded
inside, along with JavaScript to provide interactivity, so that the user can
perform basic «tactile» enquires over the plot, such as zooming, panning,
mouseovering the elements to get the tooltip with exact values and so on. The
sample of this idea can be seen on [0], however they are a bit lush with
graphics, because that's what they are showcasing.

I wonder if this idea seems plausible to R's developpers and whether I should
develop it into a full proposal?

Thanks in advance.

[0]: http://raphaeljs.com/analytics.html
--
Oleksiy Protas
National University «Kyiv-Mohyla Academy»

messages.subject: Re: Proposal idea: Interactive visualisations with SVG/HTML5 instead of Java
parts:
Hello,

On Sunday, April 01, 2012 11:22:50 PM you wrote:
> I strongly recommend focusing on HTML5 / JavaScript canvas outputs for R
Let me develop it a bit further, the benefits of canvas are mostly:
- speed, efficiency
- pixel-based nature which instanly resolves the zooming out artifacts problem
However, canvas:
- lacks a scene graph, which prevents it from being used in a nice event-based
interface and implies making own window-widget system inside, though there are
perhaps many libraries for that already
- has to be redrawn every time, since it's essentialy a framebuffer, while one
could manipulate the graph of SVG in a more sophisticated manner

Now, I assume there aren't HTML5 plotting implementations for R so far since
you recommend me, thus what I would like to do given those constraints, your
recommendation and the idea:
- Creating a package which would provide a graphical device for mixed
SVG/Canvas plot -
1) The framework of the plot is an SVG construct. Inside a <foreignObject> is
embedded which represents a HTML5 canvas. This tag allows us to embed pretty
much anything renderable by browser inside an SVG.
2) The axes, headings, labels and so on are drawn as an SVG, this allows us to
relieve us from some of the redrawing work as well as optimize some of the
text and vector rendering since the browser obviously knows how to do that
more effiently than drawing it inside the canvas each time. Moreover, there
are some visually disinguishable UI elements, like buttons and legend present
which allows user to manipulate the plot display: zoom, highlighting,
remapping colours, showing-hiding individual sets of data and so on.
3) The plot itself is drawn by a dygraphs-derived (see below) code inside the
canvas under the «UI» SVG overlay. This approach would certainly win over
SVGannotaion in the big and complex plots since we both won't be tasked with
displaying anything over the screen resolution and we can use software anti-
aliasing and other techniques to prevent the unwanted zooming artifacts from
being shown.
4) The UI controls described below are programmed with JS functions to
manipulate the display in the way the user wants it to, those functions call
the dygraphs code back, but are in turn event handlers from the SVG elements
which relives us from pixel-hunting and reinventing the wheel of a windowing
system described above (disdvantage of canvas #1).
5) If the user desires so, the current state of his work with the plot can be
rendered by the same Java Script either in a raster image with a specified
resolution, or they could produce a true vector svg version out of it, so that
they could save the image for inclusion into a printed work in the exact state
they achieved with their manipulation.
6) Additionally fix the compatibility issues with SVGAnnotation if there turns
out to be any and tune it's look and feel to be consistent with that of the
canvas/svg solution.

Should I try with such a proposal?

> Perhaps an interface to http://dygraphs.com/ graphs?
From what I've just seen about them, R can natively produce much more types of
plots than they support, but they definitely look astonishing. Since it its an
opensource JavaScript library one could get it into R package and write the
glue code, enrich it with features we would like it to support and commit the
changes back to them as well.

> SVGAAnnotation doesn't work well with most browsers -- how about
> getting it working with Chrome, Firefox, and IE?
That can be done as well, but in my experience with Chromium it did work quite
well. Is there an issue tracker for it, or someplace where one can see the
issues list?

--
Oleksiy Protas
National University «Kyiv-Mohyla Academy»

messages.subject: Re: Proposal idea: Interactive visualisations with SVG/HTML5 instead of Java
parts:
Oleksiy,

I've been following this thread with interest.

Here are some more ideas:

I like the idea of interactive graphics that are still interactive when
R isn't available. For example, R might output and SVG with embedded
JavaScript that may be rendered and interactive using a web browser.
I've been doing this for some time by hand-editing the SVGs output by
R's svg device. See the attached file for example; open in a browser
(Chrome works best, v8 is awesome) and drag one of the gray bars within
the plot.

In fact, the gridSVG package for R allows us to add JavaScript to SVG
graphics. I believe that the attached graphic could have been created
using gridSVG.

But, the gridSVG mechanism isn't that sophisticated. It would really
facilitate the process if we had a "grammer of interactive graphics" a
la the "grammer of graphics". For instance, suppose we plot a circle
with radius r and a point with coordinates (x,y). Additionally, we want
these objects to be movable (draggable) within the plot, be to ensure
that the radius r is identical in value to the coordinate x. Hence, by
interacting with the point - by dragging it along the x-axis - we would
also affect the circle radius, and vice versa. It would be really cool
to have a sub-language to specify this and similar types of
associations. I think of the SVG+JavaScript mechanism as a back-end to
this type of grammar; just one way to render the interactive graphic.
There may be other back ends, ones that depend on R, and ones that
don't.

Regards,
Matt

messages.author: aefc4fa86732afa5
messages.subject: Re: Proposal idea: Interactive visualisations with SVG/HTML5 instead of Java
parts:
Hi all,

About ~2 years ago I was considering submitting a GSOC proposal on a similar topic. I wrote a basic package to do some plotting, if that's at all useful: http://www.techpolicy.ca/?p=95

Happy to chat and mentor anyone going through on this. I think it's an extremely important addition to the R portfolio. Depending on which browsers you want to support, d3 might be a good (http://mbostock.github.com/d3/) or Protovis (some folks have written IE-supported plugins for this too, though it doesn't support IE out of the box). I'm a big fan of jQuery-based plotting tools, and my own plugin was using Raphael -- http://raphaeljs.com/

Happy to contribute or help where I can.

Thanks,
Wojciech

Canopy Labs Inc.: automating customer analytics to drive revenue growth

messages.subject: Re: Proposal idea: Interactive visualisations with SVG/HTML5 instead of Java
parts:
Hello all,

Since there are three letters above me, I'll first answer them and then sum up
some additional ideas, so this might be a long read. Thank you for all the
replies, they were quite insightful.

On Wednesday, April 04, 2012 11:42:29 PM you wrote:
> Note there is http://www.rforge.net/canvas/ and http://www.rgraph.net/
> but they produce non-interactive graphics, unlike dygraphs.com -- you
> could propose to add some of the features of dygraphs to those two
> packages ("if time permits"), but it would be easier to simply produce
> a package which generates dygraphs graphs, as you have suggested.
I've glanced both, but it seems like building a new thing with all things said
here in mind is easier. Afer all, HTML5 canvas API isn't a terribly
challenging part, but the organisation and the exact makeup of interactivity
is as far as I see the problem.

> Also you might want to have a look at
> http://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iSXNfZESR5I from Hadley Wickham, a
> fellow mentor and creator of the ggplot2 package, which you could also
> consider proposing to enhance with interactive javascript. But watch
> that video first.
Thank you for sharing this video, I've even downloaded in from youtube. I was
especially thrilled with linked plots (the crime thing), it should really be
the way to go with interactive infographics I suppose. They seem to have gone
native implementation instead, so it would only make sense to catch up these
ideas as well as the whole ggplot2 thing with an environment agonistic JS
implementation, so that we relieve ourselves some part of the problem. In fact
we're speaking here about the whole alternative canvas widget from what they
are using, however their way [Qt] has some links to ECMAScripts still, so it
might be interesting to grow something portable across both the browser and a
specialized widget.

> And I think your project would be more likely to be
> accepted if it simply produced digraphs.com graphs, perhaps with an
> interface similar to ggplot2.
So, would this work: we take the API of ggplot2, but implement it in
HTML5/Canvas/SVG/JavaScript?

> But the important part now is to get a proposal in before the
> deadline. (Revisions can be made after the deadline.)
I will try to file it now then.

On Thu, Apr 5, 2012 at 1:15 PM, Matt Shotwell <biost...@gmail.com> wrote:
> I like the idea of interactive graphics that are still interactive when
> R isn't available. For example, R might output and SVG with embedded
> JavaScript that may be rendered and interactive using a web browser.
> I've been doing this for some time by hand-editing the SVGs output by
> R's svg device. See the attached file for example; open in a browser
> (Chrome works best, v8 is awesome) and drag one of the gray bars within
> the plot.

That was the original idea behind this thread and it still is including the
Canvas part for it might really outshine SVG on some plots (and be outshined
by it on another). This very point leads to an interesting conclusion that we
may have the three cases for the user:
a) Full CGI-like implementation, whereas the in-browser JS would query the
server process the data and display it the way jQuery works.
b) Offline implementation, which has all the factual data inside the webpage
already, this can be saved and viewed later, emailed etc.
c) Printing snapshot of a current state of the plot, which has to be mostly
vector because of the resolution requirements.
We can actually have an implementation which support all three: the usual mode
would be "a" to save resources and relieve the hard work to the C routines
inside R, then the user may want to switch the page to offline mode
effectively producing a page in "b" mode and a specific button to export the
current workspace state as a vector SVG, "c". Both "a" and "b" modes would use
a mix of SVG and Canvas depending on what's more profitable.

> But, the gridSVG mechanism isn't that sophisticated. It would really
> facilitate the process if we had a "grammer of interactive graphics" a
> la the "grammer of graphics". For instance, suppose we plot a circle
> with radius r and a point with coordinates (x,y). Additionally, we want
> these objects to be movable (draggable) within the plot, be to ensure
> that the radius r is identical in value to the coordinate x. Hence, by
> interacting with the point - by dragging it along the x-axis - we would
> also affect the circle radius, and vice versa. It would be really cool
> to have a sub-language to specify this and similar types of
> associations. I think of the SVG+JavaScript mechanism as a back-end to
> this type of grammar; just one way to render the interactive graphic.
> There may be other back ends, ones that depend on R, and ones that
> don't.

That looks good to me and it's some sort of what I had in mind when writing
here. The Canvas idea, however, is very sound as well, considering the fact
that onscreen displaying of complex plots might require more raster work than
SVG would allow us to. This essentially splits the plot into the two parts,
the interactive SVG part and a drawn Canvas one, much like I've described in
an earlier letter.

On Thursday, April 05, 2012 08:21:37 PM Wojciech Gryc wrote:
> Happy to chat and mentor anyone going through on this. I think it's an
> extremely important addition to the R portfolio. Depending on which
> browsers you want to support, d3 might be a good (
> http://mbostock.github.com/d3/) or Protovis (some folks have written
> IE-supported plugins for this too, though it doesn't support IE out of the
> box). I'm a big fan of jQuery-based plotting tools, and my own plugin was
> using Raphael -- http://raphaeljs.com/

I really like how D3 looks and Raphael is what I began with. We can cherry-
pick the best ideas from them, since implementing ggplot2 API would require
slightly more that the both currently provide.

Right now my ideas can be summarized as:
- We implement ggplot2 API with a different underlying graphical device.
- The output is flexible, it may be online, relieving the viewport culling and
optimization tasks to the R Server code, however the user will have both the
possibility to generate a standalone page and pure-vector snapshots.
- The backbone is SVG providing a carcass of all the widget and some of the
output whereas Canvas is used for pixelwisework wherever proven to produce
more reasonable onscreen output.
- Raphael, D3 and dygraphs are a way to derive JS-specific code from, since no
one of them would provide us readily with everything needed.
- As a fresh idea derived from the video, we may actually benefit from
OpenGL/WebGL inside the canvas, so it might be reasonable to outsource some
part of graphical code there in the systems which support it. SVG can still be
drawn over as an overlay.

--
Oleksiy Protas
National University «Kyiv-Mohyla Academy»

Post Scriptum:
Williams and Holland's Law:
If enough data is collected, anything may be proven by statistical
methods.
